story_text.value:
Double-click or press N to start a new experiment.

I built hexBOTs, an unusual cellular automaton based on deterministic robots.

The robots behave a bit like robotic lawnmowers, moving through their environment and reacting according to their individual rules.

The robots themselves are fully deterministic — no random functions are used while they are running. What makes them different is their “genetics”: each robot's behavior is defined by a randomly generated genome, which allows for an enormous number of different robot types.

Randomness creates the robots, but it doesn't drive them.

Once an experiment starts, everything follows deterministically from the generated genomes and the initial state. What fascinates me is the complexity that emerges from these relatively simple machines interacting with each other and their environment.

Controls:

B — enable/disable robots (also: hold mouse/finger down)

R — restart

N — new experiment (also: mouse/finger double-click)

D — save as picture

I — show information / controls

title.value: Show HN: HexBOTs – a cellular automaton with robotic lawnmowers

story_text.value:
I got tired of trying to go backpacking and losing out on permits either through lottery or someone effectively bid-sniping cancellations. So, I built a real-time alert system across every state and federal booking system in the US. This covers ~700 permitted trails and locations as well as campsites.

It's the first real end-to-end product I've ever built myself and I gotta say, it's a lot of fun. I had to build a ton of custom infra and adapters to connect to the various, disparate booking systems in order to find cancellation.

Definitely pushed my capabilities.

Hope this helps some of you finally land a trip you've been wanting to take.

Edit: I've created a forecast model for openings which has been quite accurate at a 7 and 14-day timespan. Next year I should be able to make this the backbone for predictive alerts. https://permitsnag.com/permit-forecasts

title.value: Show HN: Get hard to get backcountry permit

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I built Zerothesis, it was inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s auto research with the basic premise: let an agent improve through active attempts on optimizing an open problem.

On Zerothesis, your agent reads a problem and its shared experiment history, tries an approach, evaluates it locally, and submits its work. Sandboxes independently rerun submissions. Verified results enter a public, signed ledger with contributor attribution, and failed attempts remain visible so others can learn from them.

Current challenges include circle and sphere packing, with an automated system for agents(and their humans) to submit and vote on new problems to surface. The focus is on problems with objective, machine-checkable results.

You can contribute using any harness paired with any model you want.

ZeroThesis is free and all the results will always be open to the internet.

To try it, send your agent: “Read https://zerothesis.com/api/skill.md and follow the instructions to join zerothesis.”

I’d appreciate feedback on the experience and suggestions for problems with objective evaluators. https://zerothesis.com

title.value: Show HN: ZeroThesis – Multiplayer Autoresearch with Agents

story_text.value:
Hi, I am Estevão, the developer of Ontoplano, a holistic life management webapp, supporting *tasks planning, todos, goals, habits, notebooks, people, inventory tracking, recipes, and more.*

I built this app because my life was spread over multiple different apps and pieces of paper. Ontoplano started as a weekly planner that I made (because I dislike sharing my life information with Google and also had nitpicks with every FOSS calendar I tried) and grew into one app for everything personal.

As said in the title, the project is completely free and open source, licensed under AGPL-3.0, for anyone who wants to run their own instance.

I run my own instance at app.ontoplano.com, for people who aren't into self hosting. On it, there are no ads, no tracking/profiling code, no telemetry, no tricks whatsoever. You can leave it at any time and take all your data with you.

I firmly believe software should empower people, not exploit them, and I hope that's just what I can provide the world with by releasing Ontoplano.

Furthermore, I also like software to be beautiful and practical. Ontoplano (self-hosted or not) comes with a Mobile app (PWA or the APK if you want the widget and prettier-looking notifications), and a MCP server for using it with AI (if you hate AI, don't worry, there is no built-in AI to opt-out of, only a MCP server you can create a token for, or not).

I implemented these two because: 1. I wanted to use it smoothly, even if I am away from home 2. Sometimes is much easier to say "Hey AI, put on Ontoplano that last week I actually slacked off and played videogames everyday" than manually doing that in a calendar, for psychological and time-consuming reasons.

Besides that, you can also: - Import your notes/todo tasks from Google Tasks, Google Keep, Obsidian, Todoist, and more in the future. - Calendar sync with Google Calendar (or other calendars) using ICS - Access your shopping list offline it, and share it with your family members (if you want to).

And there is more in the roadmap. Any help is appreciated — be it you self-hosting to help me find bugs and improve the app, be it you giving me a star on GitHub.

Thank you for your attention.

Main website: https://ontoplano.com Demo (no signup, throwaway account): https://demo.ontoplano.com Code: https://github.com/ontoplano/ontoplano Docs: https://docs.ontoplano.com

story_text.value:
I’ve been building Layerz, a visual builder for native UIKit iOS apps — no code, and it runs live with no build step.

What’s different from the usual no-code/app-builder stuff:

- It renders real UIKit components (not a web view or HTML wrapper), so previews behave like the real thing.

- Action Flow: a visual sequence for app behavior — navigation, data manipulation, number/text comparisons, and branching (“if this, then that”, plus per-HTTP-status branches).

- Real API integration: import an OpenAPI 3.x / Swagger 2.0 spec (or JSON Schema) from a file or URL; it generates data schemes + endpoints, with auth, retries, and per-status response parsing. Bind responses straight to the UI.

- Zero build time: design and run on the same canvas; switch device/theme on the fly. Works on iPhone, iPad, and Mac (Catalyst).

The document is the spec itself (saved as a .layerz file), so an app is fully described by data, not generated code.

Happy to go deep on the architecture (it’s split into a pure model layer + a UIKit/SwiftUI hybrid editor). Feedback and hard questions welcome — especially on where a no-code native approach breaks down.

story_text.value:
Hey HN!

Long time reader here. I recently spent over five months to modernize an old website I have been working on since 2008: https://whatthemovie.com. This is a simple game where people uploads screenshots from movies, and other players have to guess the title of the movie from where the image was taken. This is really images from movie scenes, not promotional stuff or whatever.

We have 70k users (but most are from the 2008-2010 area so inactive), and more than 600k images uploaded by our users for 18 years. Around 30k movies in the database too.

Thanks to LLMs I was about to modernize the stack which was in an awful state (Rails 4.2, Ruby 2.4 Spaghettis code, Protoytype.js and CSS code directly in HTML etc). It was exhausting to do all the refactoring and modernization but at the end I'm happy with the result.

We also have now "Daily challenges" (like Wordle or framed.wtf) where every day a new challenge is posted and players have to find the title of the movie with a different type of challenge everyday (unzoom, cuts, focus..). It doesn't need an account at all: https://whatthemovie.com/daily

We also have "closed contests" in the vault: basically we organize temporary contests where all shots uploaded must match a specific criteria (a decade, a genre, "emotions", "cities", "phones" etc) : https://whatthemovie.com/vault

Stack is simple: Bare metal on Hetzner, images on AWS S3, docker compose with around 10 micro services (Redis, MariaDB, AI sidecar in Python, Opensearch..). A little Ansible playbook to provision the machine. New relic for performance, Rollbar to track errors. I mainly used Claude models to do the work with sometimes other models to questionate the original review of the Claude model or to try to find things the other model didn't.

Thanks for your attention, and happy to answer any questions you may have!

Yann

story_text.value:
I've made myself a timer + website blocker chrome extension to help me focus. Yes, there are dozens of extensions like this already, yet somehow none of them did quite what I wanted.

Which is: you set a timer, and the extension blocks your chosen websites, while you're trying to finally get some work done. Not much more to it.

To list some features of any note:

  - it's kinda neat
  - it doesn't redirect your tabs, so they're intact when your session ends
  - the timer can count down from a set time or up until you stop it
  - entirely local, no external requests whatsoever
  - mostly vibe-coded (but I've read through the code, and so can you)
GitHub: https://github.com/campugnatus/cucumbero

Perhaps someone else will find it useful.

story_text.value:
I wanted to improve Hindi retrieval quality, particularly for longer documents ( as the current architectures don't really have a longer context length ), and was curious how far can I push a 4090 haha :)

So I trained a Hindi-first ModernBERT from scratch:

188M parameters ~28.5B Hindi tokens 8,192-token context, one of the first Hindi encoders to support 8K context ( directly benefits the retrieval capacity, for which encoder models are used for )

1× RTX 4090 (24GB) ~5 days of training

After DPR fine-tuning, it achieves SOTA on the Hindi retrieval benchmarks I evaluated:

mMARCO Hindi: 0.2825 nDCG@10 MLDR Hindi: 0.2635 nDCG@10

The MLDR result is particularly interesting because it evaluates long-document retrieval, where the 8K context window can actually be used.

It also achieves:

Hindi NER: 0.8001 F1 MASSIVE Hindi intent: 0.4731 Macro-F1

Model and evaluation details:

https://huggingface.co/kkkamur07/hindi-modernbert

https://github.com/kkkamur07/indic-modernBERT

My goal is to extend this to a lot of low resource languages, I would be really grateful for feedback and collaboration opportunities ;) so that I can improve this even further.

1× RTX 4090 (24GB) ~5 days of training

After DPR fine-tuning, it achieves SOTA on the Hindi retrieval benchmarks I evaluated:

mMARCO Hindi: 0.2825 nDCG@10 MLDR Hindi: 0.2635 nDCG@10

The MLDR result is particularly interesting because it evaluates long-document retrieval, where the 8K context window can actually be used.

It also achieves:

Hindi NER: 0.8001 F1 MASSIVE Hindi intent: 0.4731 Macro-F1

Model and evaluation details:

https://huggingface.co/kkkamur07/hindi-modernbert

https://github.com/kkkamur07/indic-modernBERT

My goal is to extend this to a lot of low resource languages, I would be really grateful for feedback and collaboration opportunities ;) so that I can improve this even further.
